Going Home

I built an AI agent app that turns hospital discharge papers into a plan a family can actually follow: a medicine timetable, phone reminders, a warning-signs card and questions for the doctor, in the family's own language.

In short

Families leave the hospital with papers full of shorthand like "1 tab PO BID", often in a language they don't read well, and they have to start managing new, changed and stopped medicines that same day. Going Home reads those papers and restates them: what to take, when, for how long, what to stop, and when to call for help. It does not diagnose, recommend treatment, change a dose or give advice. When the papers are unclear, it asks instead of guessing. Plain code checks every dose, date and phone number against the original before anything reaches the family. My test results are 100% on five synthetic cases. That is a test on five cases, not a guarantee, and section 6 lists what can still go wrong.

2. Motivation

Before Yale, I worked with the Clinton Health Access Initiative in Cambodia, Indonesia and Laos on how governments plan and pay for health programs. A lot of that job was translation: taking a plan written for one audience and making it usable for the people who had to act on it. When I started this project I kept coming back to the most personal version of that problem, the moment a patient is sent home.

Take Mr. Chen, one of my synthetic cases. He is 79 and just had a mini-stroke caused by a new irregular heartbeat. He goes home with two new medicines, two changed doses, two things he must stop (aspirin and a ginkgo supplement, because both raise bleeding risk with his new blood thinner), five follow-up visits and tests, and a list of stroke and bleeding warning signs. The papers are written the way real ones are: "1 tab PO BID", "QHS", a hospital course full of abbreviations. His daughter manages his care, and she reads simplified Chinese best.

Today she has the printout, a patient portal that shows the same text, a call to the pharmacy, or a chatbot that might get a dose wrong. The research says this hand-off is where people get hurt. About 1 in 5 patients has an adverse event within weeks of discharge, and two-thirds of those involve medicines1. In one study, patients did not understand 82% of the medicines they had been told to stop and 69% of their dose changes2. In an emergency department study, 78% of patients misunderstood part of their instructions, and they noticed only 20% of the time4. Only 20% of family caregivers even get 24 hours' notice of a discharge6. For families who don't read English well, the risks are higher still (section 7).

So I set myself a narrow question: can AI take the papers a family already has and turn them into a plan they can follow, in their language, without ever adding anything the doctor didn't write?

3. What is new here

I looked at what a family can use today:

OptionWhat it does wellWhat it does not do
Printed After Visit Summary or patient portal (e.g., Epic MyChart)The official record, always availableSame hard text and abbreviations, no timetable, usually English only. 81% of standard instructions are above a sixth-grade reading level32
Medication reminder apps (e.g., Medisafe)30Good reminders and caregiver alertsThe family types in every medicine, dose and time; nothing reads the discharge papers or checks them
General chatbots (ChatGPT and similar)Can explain a photo of the papers in many languagesNothing checks that doses match the source, and there is no schedule, calendar or chart
Machine translation (e.g., Google Translate)Fast, many languagesLiteral; in one study 8% of translated Chinese discharge sentences could cause significant harm12
Hospital-side AI summaries (Epic features, research tools)31Plain-language summaries for clinicians to reviewBuilt for the hospital; studies found omissions and medicines not in the source29

What I think is different: Going Home is built for the family at home, it produces things they can act on (a timetable, reminders, a fridge chart) rather than more text, and it checks itself against the source. Every item has to be found in the original document and every number has to match exactly before it reaches the timetable. That verification layer is the part I spent the most time on, because the research on AI discharge summaries shows exactly the failure it prevents. To be honest about novelty: translation, plain language and reminders each exist somewhere. What's new is putting them together with checks that make the result safe enough to act on.

4. The agents: how I built it

My first list of ideas was too abstract: tools for ministries and analysts. I wanted something a family could use the day they get home, and something I could build and test without collecting anyone's data. Discharge papers fit: the input is the family's own document. I built it in Python (FastAPI, plain JavaScript front end) on my Claude subscription through the Claude Code CLI. Partway through, my university account's command-line access was switched off, and I had to wait until access came back before I could run anything for real.

The design rule I settled on early: AI reads and explains; code checks.

Figure 1. Teal boxes are Claude agents; dashed boxes are plain Python.

AgentWhat it doesTools and inputsModel and why
Transcriber (photos only)Copies every line of a photo or scan into textThe imageSonnet: transcription is straightforward
ReaderExtracts medicines (status, strength, dose, schedule, taper steps, dates, daily limits), appointments, warning signs and unclear items, each with the exact sentence it came fromThe cleaned document, fenced as untrusted data; a strict JSON schemaOpus: this is the one step where a mistake becomes a wrong dose
CheckerIndependently compares the plan with the document, looking for missed medicines, wrong values, or a stopped medicine shown as activeReal tools it calls itself from an MCP server: list_medication_lines, search_document, check_quote, verify_itemSonnet: a second, different model gives an independent view at lower cost
ExplainerWrites everything in plain words, at about a fifth-grade level, in the chosen languageOnly the verified items and their verified source sentences, never the full documentSonnet: strong multilingual writing at lower cost

The orchestrator runs these as a fixed pipeline with one controlled loop. After the Reader, code checks every quote and number. Then the Checker and the Explainer run in parallel, because the Explainer usually doesn't need to wait. If code or the Checker finds a problem, the Reader gets one repair round with the exact problems listed. Anything still unresolved stays off the timetable and is shown as "check with your care team". I chose a fixed pipeline over free-form agent chat because every step had to be predictable and capped. The Checker runs its own tool loop on an MCP server loaded with that run's document and plan, under a hard dollar cap. In the Chinese run below it made 5 tool calls:

#Tool the Checker calledInputResult
1list_medication_lines9 lines
2verify_itemm6{"verified": true, "score": 1.0, "problems": []}
3verify_itemm1{"verified": true, "score": 1.0, "problems": []}
4check_quoteCall 911 right away (BE FAST) if: face drooping on one side; arm or le{"found": true, "match": 1.0}
5check_quoteCall the Neurology Clinic at (203) 555-0150 if: a nosebleed or bleedin{"found": true, "match": 1.0}

What the first real runs taught me. Three things changed the design. First, my number check rejected "2 times a day" as an invented number, even though "twice daily" was verified, so I taught it that verified frequencies can be written as numbers. Second, my prompt-injection filter deleted a real line from the Chinese case, "Aspirin: STOP. You are now on apixaban", because "you are now" is a classic attack phrase. Losing a STOP instruction is the worst thing this app could do, so I narrowed the filter and added a test that it never happens again. Third, giving the Checker tools made it both more careful and cheaper: average cost fell from $0.25 to $0.20 per plan, and repair rounds from 1 of 5 cases to 0.

Per family per month that is about $0.40. For a hospital with around 15,000 discharges a year (my estimate for a 300-bed hospital), one plan per discharge costs about $2,964 a year at list prices.

How I kept the cost down. I used Opus only for the Reader and Sonnet for everything else. The Explainer gets the verified items rather than the whole document. Static system prompts are cached: running the same safety-test file twice dropped from $0.146 to $0.086. The Explainer runs alongside the Checker instead of after it. Repairs only happen when a check fails, and are capped at one round. And giving the Checker tools cut both cost and repairs, as described above.

Did cutting cost hurt quality? I ran the whole pipeline with the cheaper Sonnet model as the Reader:

Reader modelPromptsCasesMedicines foundField accuracyFirst-read problemsRepair roundsAvg cost
Opus (chosen)final5100%100%00/5$0.198
Sonnetfinal5100%100%11/5$0.182
Sonnetbefore my fixes4100%100%62/4$0.226

Final accuracy didn't suffer, but the cheaper Reader needed 1 repair round(s) where Opus needed 0. Before I tightened the prompts it was worse: it paraphrased instructions and once invented an "8 days" duration for a steroid taper. The code check caught all of it, but every catch cost a repair. With the gap now only $0.016 per plan, I kept Opus for the step where mistakes become wrong doses. READER_MODEL=sonnet switches it if a hospital needs the savings at scale.

6. Safety

It plans; it never prescribes

The most important safety decision was scope. Going Home restates the hospital's instructions and is not allowed to add to them. Six safeguards enforce that, and the first five are code, not instructions to the AI:

  1. Nothing reaches the timetable unless it was found in the papers. Each medicine's quoted sentence must be in the document (at least a 90% match), and its strength, dose, frequency, duration, dates and phone numbers must appear in that sentence exactly. Anything that fails goes back to the Reader once, and if it still fails it is shown only under "check with your care team".
  2. The timetable is built by code. Doses on the clock come straight from verified data, so a translation slip cannot change a dose.
  3. The Explainer cannot add numbers. Any explanation containing a number that isn't in the verified data is replaced with the hospital's own sentence. This works in any script, including Chinese and Hindi digits.
  4. The Explainer cannot add purposes or advice. A "what it's for" line appears only if the papers state a purpose, and a medicine shows no more tips than the papers' own extra instructions. In a test, an invented purpose and an invented "avoid grapefruit juice" tip were both removed.
  5. Unclear means ask. Orders like "take as directed" are never scheduled. They become questions for the doctor.
  6. The original is one tap away. Every medicine card shows the hospital's exact sentence and whether it matched.

What can still go wrong

Remaining riskWhat the app doesWhat is left
The papers contain an errorRestates them and shows the sourceThe error is repeated. The app doesn't judge doses or check interactions, by design.
Both agents miss a medicineThe Checker lists every medicine-like line with a code tool; one repair roundAn unusually written medicine could be missed. It didn't happen in my tests.
A translation changes meaningNumbers, purposes and tip counts are checked by code; the original sentence is shownThe wording itself isn't machine-checked. Next step: a back-translation check.
Clock times differ from what the care team intendsA note says times are suggestions; keep the spacingThe family adjusts.
Doubled doses on discharge dayThe first day reminds the family to ask which doses were already givenDepends on the family asking.
A photo is misreadPhoto-based plans warn the family to compare each dose with the paperQuotes are checked against the transcription, not the image. One real photo test read all 8 medicines correctly.

Attacks, malfunctions and overspending

RiskWhat I builtEvidence
Prompt injection hidden in a PDF (white or tiny text)Removed by code before any agent reads the file, then shown to the userSafety-test file (below); automated test
Visible injection ("AI assistant: ignore your checks")The whole sentence is removed, even across line breaks; the document is fenced as untrusted dataScreenshot; tests
An agent invents a dose, or the Checker invents a problemQuote and number check with one repair round; unverified items never reach the timetable; Checker claims must quote the document or are droppedTests; real repairs in the evaluation
Loops and runaway callsAt most 1 repair round, 8 model calls and a hard dollar cap per agent call; the Checker may use only its four toolsTests
Overspending150,000-token cap per plan; 40 plans per day; upload limits; timeoutsTests. The daily cap actually stopped my own recording script on its 41st plan of the day.
Unsafe output in the page; privacyAll model text is escaped; papers aren't saved and logs keep token counts onlyCode

7. Impact: could this save lives?

My thesis: most of the harm after discharge doesn't come from missing medicine. It comes from a plan that doesn't survive the trip home. It fails at four points: the family doesn't understand what changed, can't read the language, can't turn the orders into a daily routine, or doesn't recognize when to get help. Going Home targets those four points with tools that each have evidence behind them. Hospitals have shown that handing patients this kind of plan reduces returns to the hospital. Going Home makes that plan automatically, in the family's language, for about 20 cents.

Where the plan breaksWhat the evidence showsWhat Going Home doesEvidence that this kind of fix works
Not understanding what changedPatients didn't understand 82% of stopped medicines and 69% of dose changes2. Medicine discrepancies at home: 14.3% readmitted vs 6.1% without3A red STOP box; "Changed" badges with old and new doses; the source sentence on every cardPharmacist counseling at discharge cut preventable drug events from 11% to 1%21
Not reading the language49% of adverse events in patients with limited English caused physical harm, vs 30%7. Chinese speakers: 1.7× the odds of readmission8The whole plan in 11 languages; numbers locked to the sourceBedside interpreter phones cut readmissions from 17.8% to 13.4%9
Turning orders into a routineOnly 15% of adults could organize a 7-medicine regimen into 4 daily times17. 66% of drug-harm hospitalizations in older adults were unintentional overdoses15Clock times for each day, tapers and end dates, "only if needed" kept off the clock, phone remindersStandard-time labels improved correct use (OR 5.08 with limited literacy)18; text reminders doubled the odds of adherence19
Missing the warning signs and follow-upOnly 44% of older patients recalled the details of their follow-up appointment5. Heart-failure weight gain starts a week before admission22. An untreated stroke destroys 1.9 million neurons a minute23A warning card (911 vs call the clinic), calendar reminders for every visit, daily-weight instructions in the planStroke-symptom education shortened delays to hospital in 10 of 13 studies24; earlier follow-up after heart failure was linked to fewer readmissions25

The strongest single piece of evidence is Project RED, a randomized trial in which patients received an "After Hospital Care Plan" with a color-coded medication schedule, an appointment calendar and what to do if a problem arises. Hospital use within 30 days fell by about 30% (0.314 vs 0.451 visits per person per month)20. That plan is almost exactly what Going Home produces, except RED needed trained staff to build it by hand for every patient.

Why the family's own language. Patients with limited English are hurt more often when something goes wrong7, are readmitted more often8, and often get their instructions interpreted by a family member11, whose errors are more likely to matter clinically10. There are 26.5 million such people in the US, and the five most common languages (Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, Korean, Tagalog) are all in Going Home14. Two honest caveats shaped the design. A small trial found that written translation alone didn't raise comprehension scores13, which is why Going Home turns the plan into a timetable and reminders rather than translating text. And machine translation can produce harmful sentences12, which is why every number is locked to the source and the original sentence is always shown.

What the scheduling actually does. A discharge order like "Prednisone 10 mg: 4 tablets on 10/17 and 10/18, then 3 tablets on 10/19 and 10/20, then 2, then 1, then stop" becomes the right dose on each calendar day, with the last day marked. "1 tab PO BID" becomes 8 AM and 8 PM, "QHS" becomes bedtime, and "1–2 tabs q6h PRN" stays off the clock with its daily limit shown. Stopped medicines get their own red box. Then it all goes to the phone as reminders. This matters most for the medicines that hurt people most: blood thinners, insulin, antiplatelets and diabetes pills cause two-thirds of emergency hospitalizations for drug harm in older adults15, and apixaban, Mr. Chen's blood thinner, is involved in about half of the emergency visits for bleeding from the newer blood thinners16.

A careful estimate. Here is what the numbers could mean for one hospital, with every assumption visible:

Per 10,000 dischargesNumberWhere it comes from
Discharges10,000a round number to make the math easy
30-day readmissions (13.9%)1,390national rate26
Drug-related (median 21%)292systematic review27
Preventable (median 69% of those)201same review27
Avoided if Going Home prevents 10%–30% of those20–60my assumption, below Project RED's ~30%20
Hospital cost avoided ($16,300 each)$0.33M–$0.98Maverage readmission cost26
Cost of running Going Home for every discharge$1,976measured: average cost per plan × 10,000

The estimate rests on one assumption I can't yet test: that Going Home prevents 10%–30% of preventable drug-related readmissions, well below what Project RED achieved with a full staff-run program. Even at the low end, the hospital cost avoided is more than a hundred times the cost of running the app. Hospitals also have a direct reason to care: Medicare withheld about $521 million in readmission penalties in a single year28.

On saving lives. I won't claim a number of lives saved. National estimates of deaths from drug harm are old, extrapolated and disputed, and I haven't run a trial. But the path from a confused discharge to a death is well documented: a doubled blood thinner becomes a bleed, a missed insulin change becomes a crisis, a stroke sign goes unrecognized while the clock runs. Of the post-discharge adverse events that caused at least temporary disability in Forster's study, about half were preventable1. Going Home is aimed squarely at that path.

A simulated reader study (AI personas, not people). Before a real test, I had three AI personas (played by Claude Haiku) answer six questions a caregiver must get right, once from the original papers and once from the Going Home plan in their language, with Claude Sonnet grading against my answer key.

Simulated reader (AI persona)Plan languageFrom the original papersFrom the Going Home plan

The scores tie overall, but the plan helped where it matters most: the daughter couldn't tell her father's evening medicines from the papers ("short words like BID and QHS that I don't understand") and could from the plan. An AI persona reads English well even when told not to, so this proxy understates the language benefit.

What a real clinic told me

I shared Going Home with a clinic on the Laos–China border. Most of its patients speak Chinese (many also speak Lao), and many of the clinic's doctors trained in China, so medicines, diagnoses and the way patients are treated are often handled in Chinese. That is why a plan in Chinese made sense there, and it's the same reason I built Mr. Chen's case around it.

What they told me: before, discharged patients often had to go back to the nurses, and pay, to get help following their treatment, or they followed it from memory. Many couldn't recall the doctor's diagnosis accurately. Having the plan written out in their own language was very helpful. Their main request was a phone app they could install and use every day.

This is informal feedback from one clinic, not a measured study: no times or scores were recorded. A measured test (time and correct answers with and without the app) is the next step; the protocol is in the repo.

8. Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet. I've tested on five synthetic cases, one attack file and one photo; real papers vary more (scans, handwriting, long tables). Clock times are defaults the family has to adjust. It doesn't check doses or interactions, so an error in the papers is repeated faithfully. A plan takes one to two minutes, longer in scripts like Hindi. Live mode needs a Claude login and runs on a computer, not a phone. The user evidence so far is informal feedback from one clinic, and the impact numbers above are estimates until a measured pilot runs.

Next: more feedback before more features. This is a first draft. Over the next month I want to collect more feedback, from the clinic that tried it and from other clinics, nurses and families, so I can see which improvements matter most. A measured test (time and correct answers with and without the app) is the first step. The ideas on my list so far: the phone app the clinic asked for, read-back questions ("what do you stop?") flagged to the care team, a back-translation check, SMS reminders, and an evaluation on de-identified real papers with a hospital partner.

Future scope. Later on, I hope to launch Going Home as an application, and as a business built around its mission. I'd like to work with foundations that support health care in developing countries, and in developed ones, so that families everywhere leave the hospital with a plan they can follow. The goal is the same one this project started with: preventing the harm, and the deaths, that happen when a care plan doesn't survive the trip home.

How I used AI, and other disclosures

I built Going Home with Claude Code as my coding assistant, and used it to help research and draft this report and the slides, as the assignment allows. I checked every number against the run logs or the cited source. All patients and documents are synthetic. The demo video is a screen recording of real runs on my computer: waits are sped up and labeled, and the narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro, an open-source text-to-speech model). The simulated reader study uses AI personas and is labeled as such throughout. The clinic feedback in section 7 is informal and reported as the clinic described it.
